title: Random Forest
abstract:
Bagging with one crucial refinement. A random forest is a collection of decision
trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample — and, unlike bagging, each
node samples its candidate features afresh from the full set. That
node-level sampling is the whole difference, and it lowers the correlation
between trees, which lowers the variance floor. This document covers the
mechanism, why the extra randomness converts LBHV into LBLV so effectively, the
hyperparameters the notes list, and the reasons random forests remain the
strongest default model for tabular data.

From the notes

Not much tuning needed in the algo.

It is an ensemble technique — a collection of decision

For data sampling, for each $D.T_1$, $D.T_2$, \ldots :
 row sampling, or column sampling, or a combination —

blocks.t: From the notes: why it performs so well

It converts LBHV $\longrightarrow$ LBLV. Noisy points' impact is
shared because of data sampling. Thus it solves the bias–variance tradeoff
issue.
The One Difference From Bagging
From the notes
In bagging and RF, for data sampling if we do column sampling:

Random Forest \newline [node-level sampling]

respective D.T / SVM.

At each node, sampling is done from the full set of columns for the

blocks.t:
Thus more randomness — and thus many times RF is better than
bagging.

blocks.cap:
The distinction. Bagging chooses a column subset once per tree, so
 every node inside that tree sees the same features. A random forest draws a
 fresh subset at every node, from the full column set.

blocks.t: Why the extra randomness matters
Recall the variance of an average (Topics 58, 60):

\operatorname{Var} \left(\frac1B\sum_b \hat f_b\right)
 =\underbrace{\rho\sigma^{2}}_{\text{floor}}+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^{2}.

Adding trees drives the second term to zero but cannot touch the
first. The only way to go lower is to reduce $\rho$ — the correlation between
trees.

Bootstrapping the rows alone leaves $\rho$ high, because if one feature is
strongly predictive nearly every tree will split on it at the root and the trees
end up looking alike. Sampling features at each node forces many trees to
build without the dominant feature at all, so they find genuinely different
structure. Random forests lower the floor, not just the second term.

blocks.cap:
Left: with a dominant feature present, bagging picks it at the root of
 almost every tree; the forest spreads the choice across many features. Right:
 the resulting accuracy — the forest converges to a better plateau because its
 variance floor is lower.

blocks.t: Two sources of randomness, not one

A random forest is bootstrap sampling of rows plus random subspace
sampling of columns at each split. Removing either weakens it: with
bootstrap=False and max_features=None a forest degenerates into
$B$ identical trees.

blocks.t: Hyperparameters
From the notes

rows: Number of trees in the forest
Minimum samples required to split a node
Minimum data points that must remain in a leaf

blocks.cap:
The three that matter most. max_features controls the
 decorrelation, bootstrap the row sampling, and
 min_samples_split the depth of the individual trees.

rows: The one that matters most. Defaults: "sqrt" for classification, $1.0$ for regression. Smaller $\Rightarrow$ more decorrelation, weaker individual trees
More is always at least as good; it only costs time. 100–500 is typical
Usually leave as None — a forest wants deep trees (Topic 60)
The gentler complexity control; 1–5 for classification, higher for regression

blocks.t: "Not much tuning needed"

The notes' remark is accurate and is a large part of why random forests are so
widely used. The defaults are close to optimal on most tabular problems, the
model is insensitive to feature scaling and monotone transforms, it handles mixed
feature types, and the only parameter that reliably repays tuning is
max_features. Compare with gradient boosting (Topic 67), where learning
rate, depth and estimator count interact and must be tuned together.
Random Forest vs Bagging
From the notes

In bagging the base estimator could be a D.T, SVM, KNN etc. In RF the
base estimator is always a D.T.

head: Bagging
Random Forest
rows: Rows only, or rows $+$ one column subset
Rows $+$ a fresh column subset per split

blocks.t: Extra Trees — one more step of randomness

ExtraTreesClassifier goes further: instead of searching for the best
threshold within the sampled features, it picks thresholds at random and
takes the best of those. Each tree is weaker and more biased, but $\rho$ falls
further and fitting is much faster. On noisy data it sometimes beats a random
forest — the same logic, pushed one notch harder.
Code

import numpy as np, time
from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestClassifier, RandomForestRegressor,
                              BaggingClassifier, ExtraTreesClassifier)
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, cross_val_score,
                                     RandomizedSearchCV)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 15))
X[:, 1] = .9*X[:, 0] + .4*rng.normal(0, 1, n)      # a correlated pair
y = (2.5*X[:, 0] + X[:, 2] - .8*X[:, 3] + .6*X[:, 2]*X[:, 3]
     + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE BASELINE COMPARISON
# =====================================================================
models = {
    "single tree":   DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
    "bagging (200)": BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(),
                                       n_estimators=200, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
    "RANDOM FOREST": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200,
                                            random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
    "extra trees":   ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=200,
                                          random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
}
print(f"{'model':16s} {'test acc':>9s} {'fit time':>10s}")
for name, m in models.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); m.fit(X_tr, y_tr); el = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"{name:16s} {m.score(X_te, y_te):9.4f} {el:9.3f}s")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE KEY DIFFERENCE -- node-level vs tree-level column sampling
# =====================================================================
bag = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=300,
                        max_features=0.5, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
rf  = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_features="sqrt",
                             random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

bag_roots = np.bincount([int(t.tree_.feature[0]) for t in bag.estimators_],
                        minlength=15)
rf_roots  = np.bincount([int(t.tree_.feature[0]) for t in rf.estimators_],
                        minlength=15)
print(f"\n{'feature':>8s} {'bagging roots':>15s} {'RF roots':>10s}")
for j in np.argsort(-bag_roots)[:6]:
    print(f"{j:8d} {bag_roots[j]:15d} {rf_roots[j]:10d}")
print(f"\nbagging: top feature is the root of "
      f"{bag_roots.max()/300:.1%} of trees")
print(f"forest : top feature is the root of {rf_roots.max()/300:.1%} of trees")
# Bagging's trees nearly all start with the same dominant feature, so they
# look alike. The forest spreads the choice -> LOWER CORRELATION.

# MEASURE the correlation between tree predictions directly:
def pairwise_corr(ens, X):
    P = np.array([t.predict(X) for t in ens.estimators_])
    C = np.corrcoef(P)
    return C[np.triu_indices_from(C, k=1)].mean()

print(f"\nmean pairwise correlation between trees:")
print(f"  bagging       {pairwise_corr(bag, X_te):.4f}")
print(f"  random forest {pairwise_corr(rf,  X_te):.4f}   <- lower = lower variance floor")

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE VARIANCE FLOOR -- rho * sigma^2
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'n_estimators':>13s} {'bagging':>9s} {'forest':>9s}")
for B in [1, 5, 25, 100, 400, 1000]:
    a = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=B,
                          random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te)
    b = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=B, random_state=0,
                               n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te)
    print(f"{B:13d} {a:9.4f} {b:9.4f}")
# Both plateau, but the FOREST plateaus higher -- adding trees kills the
# (1-rho)/B term; only lower rho moves the floor.

# =====================================================================
# 4. max_features IS THE PARAMETER THAT MATTERS
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'max_features':>13s} {'cv acc':>9s} {'tree corr':>11s} {'fit time':>10s}")
for mf in [1, 2, "sqrt", "log2", 6, 10, None]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, max_features=mf,
                               random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    el = time.perf_counter() - t0
    s = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, max_features=mf,
                                               random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
                        X_tr, y_tr, cv=4, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    print(f"{str(mf):>13s} {s:9.4f} {pairwise_corr(m, X_te):11.4f} {el:9.3f}s")
# Small max_features -> low correlation but individually weak trees.
# max_features=None -> the forest degenerates towards bagging.
print(f"\ndefault for classification is 'sqrt': sqrt(15) = {np.sqrt(15):.2f} features")

# =====================================================================
# 5. BOTH SOURCES OF RANDOMNESS ARE NEEDED
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'configuration':38s} {'test acc':>9s} {'tree corr':>11s}")
for tag, kw in [
    ("rows + node columns  (standard RF)", dict(bootstrap=True,  max_features="sqrt")),
    ("rows only            (= bagging)",   dict(bootstrap=True,  max_features=None)),
    ("node columns only",                  dict(bootstrap=False, max_features="sqrt")),
    ("NEITHER (identical trees)",          dict(bootstrap=False, max_features=None)),
]:
    m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0,
                               n_jobs=-1, **kw).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{tag:38s} {m.score(X_te, y_te):9.4f} {pairwise_corr(m, X_te):11.4f}")
# With NEITHER, every tree is identical: correlation ~1.0 and the ensemble
# is just one tree computed 200 times.

# =====================================================================
# 6. IT CONVERTS LBHV INTO LBLV
# =====================================================================
def bias_variance(make_model, sims=80):
    grid = rng.normal(0, 1, (300, 15))
    grid[:, 1] = .9*grid[:, 0] + .4*rng.normal(0, 1, 300)
    truth = (2.5*grid[:,0] + grid[:,2] - .8*grid[:,3] + .6*grid[:,2]*grid[:,3] > 0)
    P = []
    for _ in range(sims):
        Xi = rng.normal(0, 1, (500, 15))
        Xi[:, 1] = .9*Xi[:, 0] + .4*rng.normal(0, 1, 500)
        yi = (2.5*Xi[:,0] + Xi[:,2] - .8*Xi[:,3] + .6*Xi[:,2]*Xi[:,3]
              + rng.normal(0, 1.1, 500) > 0).astype(int)
        P.append(make_model().fit(Xi, yi).predict(grid))
    P = np.array(P)
    return np.mean((P.mean(0) - truth)**2), np.mean(P.var(0))

print(f"\n{'model':22s} {'Bias^2':>9s} {'Variance':>10s} {'label':>8s}")
for tag, mk in [("single deep tree", lambda: DecisionTreeClassifier()),
                ("bagging (50)",     lambda: BaggingClassifier(
                                        DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=50)),
                ("random forest (50)", lambda: RandomForestClassifier(
                                        n_estimators=50, n_jobs=-1))]:
    b2, v = bias_variance(mk)
    lab = "LBHV" if v > 0.10 else "LBLV"
    print(f"{tag:22s} {b2:9.4f} {v:10.4f} {lab:>8s}")
# Bias barely moves; variance collapses. LBHV -> LBLV, as the notes say.

# =====================================================================
# 7. "NOT MUCH TUNING NEEDED"
# =====================================================================
default = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
    {"n_estimators":      [100, 300, 600],
     "max_features":      [1, 2, "sqrt", "log2", 6, None],
     "max_depth":         [None, 8, 16, 32],
     "min_samples_split": [2, 5, 10, 20],
     "min_samples_leaf":  [1, 2, 4, 8],
     "bootstrap":         [True, False]},
    n_iter=40, cv=4, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(f"\ndefaults      test {default.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"tuned (40 fits) test {search.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"gain: {search.score(X_te, y_te) - default.score(X_te, y_te):+.4f}")
print("best:", search.best_params_)
# The gain is usually small -- which is exactly the notes' point.

# =====================================================================
# 8. NO SCALING NEEDED, AND IT HANDLES BOTH TASKS
# =====================================================================
Xs = X.copy(); Xs[:, 0] *= 10_000
print(f"\nRF on unscaled data: "
      f"{cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1), Xs, y, cv=4).mean():.4f}")
print(f"RF on scaled data  : "
      f"{cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1), StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xs), y, cv=4).mean():.4f}")

yr = X[:, 0]*2 + X[:, 2] - .5*X[:, 3]**2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
Xr_tr, Xr_te, yr_tr, yr_te = train_test_split(X, yr, test_size=.3, random_state=0)
rfr = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(Xr_tr, yr_tr)
print(f"\nRandomForestRegressor R2: {rfr.score(Xr_te, yr_te):.4f}")
print(f"single tree R2          : "
      f"{DecisionTreeClassifier.__mro__ and 0 or 0:.0f}",
      f"{__import__('sklearn.tree', fromlist=['DecisionTreeRegressor']).DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0).fit(Xr_tr, yr_tr).score(Xr_te, yr_te):.4f}")
print(f"regressor default max_features is 1.0, classifier's is 'sqrt'")
Worked Examples
Feature subsampling in a random forest
A dataset with $p = 16$ features.
Step 1 – features tried at each split. Classification default: $\lfloor\sqrt{p}\rfloor = \sqrt{16} = 4$. Regression default: $\lfloor p/3\rfloor = \lfloor 5.33\rfloor = 5$.
Step 2 – what a single split sees. Each split chooses its best feature from a random subset of 4 of the 16 features. A node therefore cannot always use the single strongest feature.

Step 3 – why that helps. Suppose one feature $F^\star$ is very strong. In plain bagging every tree would split on it at the top, so all trees look alike and their errors are correlated. With $m=4$, $F^\star$ is available at only about $4/16 = 25\%$ of splits, so other features get used, the trees decorrelate, and averaging reduces variance more.

Two randomisations in total. Rows: bootstrap sample per tree (from bagging). Columns: a fresh random subset of $m$ features at every split. Both are needed; row sampling alone leaves trees too similar.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Random forest is a supervised algorithm that works for both
 regression and classification, is an ensemble — a collection of
 decision trees, and is a bagging technique.

For data sampling it uses row sampling, column sampling, or a
 combination, with or without replacement.

The key difference from bagging: bagging samples columns
 once per tree (tree-level), so every node inside a tree sees the
 same subset. A random forest samples at each node, from the full
 set of columns — thus more randomness, and
 thus many times RF is better than bagging.

That extra randomness lowers the correlation $\rho$ between trees, and
 since the variance of an average is $\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$,
 it lowers the floor — something more trees can never do.

It converts LBHV into LBLV: noisy points' impact is shared
 because of the data sampling, so it solves the bias–variance
 tradeoff.

In bagging the base estimator could be D.T, SVM, KNN; in RF it is
 always a decision tree.

Hyperparameters: bootstrap (True/False),
 n_estimators, max_depth,
 min_samples_split, max_features,
 min_samples_leaf — chosen by Grid Search CV or
 Randomized Search CV.

Not much tuning is needed — max_features is the only
 parameter that reliably repays it.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What is the difference between bagging and a random forest?

Two things. The base estimator is always a decision tree, and — the important
one — column sampling happens at every node rather than once per tree.
That node-level sampling means many trees are forced to build without the dominant
feature, which decorrelates them.

Q. Why does decorrelating the trees matter more than adding more of
them?

Because the variance of an average is $\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$.
Adding trees drives the second term to zero but leaves $\rho\sigma^2$ untouched.
Only reducing the correlation lowers that floor — which is exactly what
node-level feature sampling does.
Q. What does max_features control, and what should it be?

How many features each split may consider. Defaults are "sqrt" for
classification and all features for regression. Smaller values decorrelate the
trees more but make each individually weaker, so there is an optimum — and it is
the one hyperparameter of a random forest that reliably repays tuning.
Q. Should you limit max_depth in a random forest?

Usually not. A forest reduces variance by averaging, so it wants deep,
high-variance, decorrelated trees. Limiting depth adds bias that averaging cannot
remove. Use min_samples_leaf if you need some control, especially for
regression.
Q. Why do random forests need so little tuning?

Because the defaults are near-optimal on most tabular data, the model is
insensitive to feature scaling and monotone transforms, more trees never hurt, and
depth is normally left unbounded. That leaves essentially one dial. Gradient
boosting, by contrast, has interacting parameters that must be tuned jointly.
Q. When would a random forest lose to gradient boosting?

When you can afford careful tuning and want the last few points of accuracy —
boosting reduces bias as well as variance and usually wins on clean tabular
benchmarks. A forest wins on robustness: it is harder to misconfigure, less
sensitive to noisy labels, parallel by construction, and gives free out-of-bag
validation.
